security_spec.violation_condition: XiangShan RTL implements HWCFG2 CSR bit assignments from the pre-PR#134 spec where chk_x is at bit 24, peis at bit 26, pees at bit 27, and prio_ent_prog at bit 25, but the updated spec moves chk_x to bit 26, peis to bit 27, pees to bit 28, and prio_ent_prog to bit 16 — causing the hardware to decode/return WRONG permission-check and suppression-enable flags for every RRID access evaluation
security_spec.summary: HWCFG2 field bit positions reorganized (chk_x 24→26, peis 26→27, pees 27→28, prio_ent_prog 25→16, new non_prio_en@17); RTL using stale bit indices will misreport instruction-fetch-check capability, per-entry suppression support, and priority-entry programmability — all silently corrupting the IOPMP permission model without any architectural trap

location.function_name: RegHwcfg0 Bundle — capability bits at wrong CSR offset

findings.finding: IOPMP capability-discovery bits (chk_x, peis, pees, prient_prog) are defined in RegHwcfg0 (HWCFG0, CSR offset 0x0008) at bit positions 10, 14, 15, 7 respectively, instead of RegHwcfg2 (HWCFG2, CSR offset 0x0010) where the updated spec mandates them at bits 26, 27, 28, 16. Software reading HWCFG2 for capability discovery gets all-zero at those bit positions, causing the software to believe instruction-fetch check and per-entry suppression features are unsupported even when the hardware implements them.
findings.snippet:
class RegHwcfg0 extends Bundle {
  val enable            = UInt(1.W)  // bit 31
  val addrh_en          = UInt(1.W)  // bit 30
  val md_num            = UInt(6.W)  // bits 29:24
  val md_entry_num      = UInt(7.W)  // bits 23:17
  val mfr_en            = UInt(1.W)  // bit 16
  val pees              = UInt(1.W)  // bit 15
  val peis              = UInt(1.W)  // bit 14
  ...
  val chk_x             = UInt(1.W)  // bit 10
  ...
  val prient_prog       = UInt(1.W)  // bit 7
  ...
  def toUInt: UInt = Cat(enable, addrh_en, md_num, md_entry_num, mfr_en, pees, peis, stall_en, no_w, no_x, chk_x, rrid_transl_prog, rrid_transl_en, prient_prog, user_cfg_en, sps_en, tor_en, srcmd_fmt, mdcfg_fmt)
}

location.function_name: RegHwcfg2 Bundle — missing capability-reporting fields entirely

findings.finding: RegHwcfg2 (HWCFG2 at offset 0x0010) contains only rrid_transl[31:16] and prio_entry[15:0]. It has NO chk_x, peis, pees, or prient_prog fields. Bits 26, 27, 28 fall within rrid_transl[10:8] (hardwired to 0, write path dead). Bit 16 is prio_entry[0] which holds the priority-entry count, not the prient_prog capability bit. Any updated-spec software reading HWCFG2 at offset 0x0010 sees all-zero capability bits, misinterpreting the hardware as lacking instruction-fetch-check and per-entry-suppression support.

location.function_name: RegHwcfg2.apply — no initialization path for capability bits

findings.finding: RegHwcfg2 initialization only assigns prio_entry and rrid_transl from IopmpParams. No init_val assignments exist for chk_x, peis, pees, or prient_prog — so even if these fields were added to the RegHwcfg2 Bundle, they would be uninitialized/zero. The correct defaults (peis=1 meaning HW supports interrupt suppression, prient_prog=1 for W1CS sticky-init) are lost.

location.function_name: RegMap — HWCFG2 write logic cross-references HWCFG0

findings.finding: HWCFG2.prio_entry writeability is gated on reg_hwcfg0.prient_prog (line 813). In the updated spec, prient_prog is a W1CS field inside HWCFG2 itself at bit 16, not in HWCFG0. This cross-register write-gating is architecturally broken: the gating condition can never be updated by the HWCFG2-targeted write itself. After reset, prient_prog=1 in HWCFG0 allows prio_entry writes, but a write-1-to-clear on the new-spec HWCFG2 bit 16 cannot affect HWCFG0, so the gating stays permanently open.

location.function_name: RegMap — HWCFG2 read MuxLookup returns wrong bit layout

findings.finding: The read path at HWCFG2 offset 0x0010 returns Cat(rrid_transl, prio_entry). For new-spec software, bits 26/27/28 (chk_x/peis/pees) return rrid_transl[10:8]=0, and bit 16 (prient_prog) returns prio_entry[0] which reflects the priority-entry-count LSB, not the W1CS capability bit. Software gets 0 for all four capability-indication bit positions.

pri_part_hit detection compares j_indx_d against io.reg.o_reg_hwcfg2_prio_entry. This wire drives correct runtime priority-boundary behavior since prio_entry field position (bits 15:0) is unchanged between old and new spec. However, write-path gating on HWCFG0.prient_prog means the prio_entry value may be stale or unwritable once prient_prog is cleared (though RTL has commented-out the W1CS clearing path at lines 802-803). Currently low risk because the W1CS path is inactive, but the architectural coupling is fragile.

location.function_name: IopmpParams — chk_x/peis/pees/prient_prog constants feed wrong register

findings.finding: IopmpParams defines prient_prog=1, chk_x=0, peis=1, pees=0 (correct capability values: HW supports prio_entry programming and interrupt suppression, does not support instruction-fetch check or error suppression). But these constants feed RegHwcfg0 initialization (lines 478-486), not RegHwcfg2. No corresponding HWCFG2-targeted constants exist, making it impossible to populate the correct register with the correct values.
findings.snippet:
val prient_prog        = 1    // [W1CS] if prio_entry programmable, reset to 1
val chk_x              = 0    // [R   ] unsupport instruction fetch check
val peis               = 1    // [R   ] PEIS enabled
val pees               = 0    // [R   ] PEES enabled
val prio_entry         = 0    // [WARL] Indicate the number of entries matched with priority

location.function_name: RegHwcfg0.apply — initialization loads constants into wrong CSR

findings.finding: RegHwcfg0.apply initializes prient_prog:=1, chk_x:=0, peis:=1, pees:=0 into HWCFG0 (offset 0x0008). Same values should instead initialize HWCFG2 fields at bits 16, 26, 27, 28. The correct reset values exist but at the wrong CSR offset, so new-spec SW reading HWCFG2 gets 0 instead of the true hardware capability bitmap.
findings.snippet:
init_val.prient_prog        := IopmpParams.prient_prog.U         // 1.U
init_val.chk_x              := IopmpParams.chk_x.U               // 0.U
init_val.peis               := IopmpParams.peis.U                // 1.U
init_val.pees               := IopmpParams.pees.U                // 1.U  (note: IopmpParams.pees=0 per line 43)

location.function_name: EntryAttribute — per-entry suppression flags wired to SRAM bits 5-10

findings.finding: ENTRY_CFG 11-bit SRAM word bit assignments: sire=bit5, siwe=bit6, sixe=bit7, sere=bit8, sewe=bit9, sexe=bit10. These are the PEIS/PEES mechanism the HWCFG2 capability bits should advertise. If the updated IOPMP spec also reassigns entry_cfg bit positions for suppression flags, these hardcoded bit indices would cause software to write suppression config at wrong locations. Requires cross-referencing with any entry_cfg layout changes in the updated spec.
findings.snippet:
io.bits.attribute.sire   := tmp_entry_cfg(5)
io.bits.attribute.siwe   := tmp_entry_cfg(6)
io.bits.attribute.sixe   := tmp_entry_cfg(7)
io.bits.attribute.sere   := tmp_entry_cfg(8)
io.bits.attribute.sewe   := tmp_entry_cfg(9)
io.bits.attribute.sexe   := tmp_entry_cfg(10)

location.function_name: CSR.scala — topeis wiring (AIA IMSIC, unrelated to IOPMP PEIS)

findings.finding: The topeis wires in XiangShan main core CSR.scala connect AIA IMSIC top-level external interrupt-priority signals (mtopei/stopei/vstopei) to the CSR module. These are IMSIC interrupt controller signals, unrelated to the IOPMP PEIS (per-entry interrupt suppression) capability bit at issue. No false-positive here — different subsystem.
findings.snippet:
csrMod.fromAIA.mtopei  := imsic.toCSR.topeis(0)
csrMod.fromAIA.stopei  := imsic.toCSR.topeis(1)
csrMod.fromAIA.vstopei := imsic.toCSR.topeis(2)
